archetypes.name: Prime-focus parabolic reflector
archetypes.summary: Axisymmetric paraboloid with the feed at the focus; the workhorse high-gain antenna.

parameters.name: illumination efficiency
parameters.description: Taper (illumination) efficiency. DERIVED from the edge taper and f/D; supply it to override.

parameters.name: spillover efficiency
parameters.description: Spillover efficiency. DERIVED from the edge taper and f/D; supply it to override.

parameters.name: edge taper
parameters.description: total illumination at the rim relative to the centre, spreading loss included

parameters.name: feed pattern exponent
parameters.description: n in 2(n+1)cos^n(theta)

synthesis.notes: edge taper = cos^(n/2)(theta0) (1 + cos theta0)/2 in amplitude, solved for n
the fraction of a 2(n+1)cos^n feed's power the dish intercepts - exact

Taper efficiency: the aperture efficiency cot^2(theta0/2) |int sqrt(G) tan(theta/2) dtheta|^2 divided by the spillover, integrated here on 4001 points. It does not use eta_spill, so overriding one leaves the other derived.

analysis.notes: theta0 = 2*arctan(1/(4*(f/D))). Checks: f/D = 0.25 gives exactly 90 deg (focus in the aperture plane), f/D = 0.5 gives 53.13 deg.
aperture blockage removes area twice over - once from the incident field and once from the scattered field - hence the square
Ruze 1966: G/G0 = exp(-(4*pi*eps_rms/lambda)^2). Exact, and the reason surface tolerance dominates at millimetre wavelengths.
The budget is itemised rather than lumped: each term is separately arguable, and lumping them hides which one is costing you the gain.
G = eta_ap*(pi*D/lambda)^2
the 100%-efficient ceiling, for reference

From the Hankel transform of the aperture field of the classic Silver model: a rotationally symmetric feed with power pattern 2(n+1)cos^n(theta), n set by the edge taper, and physical-optics aperture theory, fitted over edge taper -20..-3 dB and f/D 0.3..1.0: within 0.02 lambda/D on the grid and on held-out points. 66.5 lambda/D at -11 dB, where the old spec asserted 70; 61 for a -3 dB taper, 74 for -20.

The FIRST sidelobe, between the first and second nulls of the same Hankel transform, fitted to 0.06 dB (0.02 on held-out points). -25.2 dB at -11 dB and f/D = 0.4. Past about -17 dB of edge taper the SECOND sidelobe becomes the higher one at larger f/D, so this stops being the peak sidelobe there.

validity: D > 10*lambda for physical-optics aperture theory to hold
the -11 dB edge taper optimum assumes the feed pattern actually achieves it; illumination and spillover efficiency trade directly against each other and only their product is meaningful
efficiency terms are defaults for a competent design, not measurements

eta_ill, eta_spill, hpbw_deg and first_sidelobe_db follow the classic Silver model: a rotationally symmetric feed with power pattern 2(n+1)cos^n(theta), n set by the edge taper, and physical-optics aperture theory; they hold for edge tapers -20..-3 dB and f/D 0.3..1.0. A real feed with unequal E- and H-plane patterns, a wandering phase centre or high cross-polarisation does worse than this ideal - supply measured efficiencies to override
at f/D = 0.25 and below the feed looks at or behind the aperture plane and no cos^n pattern reaches a finite edge taper; the derived terms are meaningless there

known_cases.source: f/D = 0.25 puts the focus exactly in the aperture plane, so the feed subtends 90 deg. Geometric identity. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 15
theta0 = 2*arctan(0.5) = 53.13 deg at f/D = 0.5. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 15
1 m dish at 10 GHz: (pi*D/lambda)^2 = 40.42 dBi at 100% efficiency. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 15
Ruze: 0.3 mm rms at 10 GHz (lambda/100) costs 0.069 dB. Ruze, Antenna Tolerance Theory, Proc. IEEE 54(4), 1966

The same 0.3 mm surface at 100 GHz (lambda = 2.9979 mm) retains only 0.2057 of the gain - a 6.87 dB loss. Ruze loss scales with (eps_rms/lambda)^2, which is why millimetre-wave dishes need precision surfaces. Ruze, Proc. IEEE 54(4), 1966
A 10% blockage diameter costs (1-0.01)^2 = 0.9801, i.e. 0.087 dB. Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 8

f/D = 0.4, -11 dB edge taper: a cos^2.271 feed. Taper and spillover by quadrature of the feed-angle integrals (scipy quad), beamwidth and first sidelobe by a numerical Hankel transform of the aperture field - not the spec's trapezoid or its fits. Gain with the default 0.98 x 0.98 cross-pol and match terms.

f/D = 0.6, -14 dB edge taper: a cos^8.277 feed. Taper and spillover by quadrature of the feed-angle integrals (scipy quad), beamwidth and first sidelobe by a numerical Hankel transform of the aperture field - not the spec's trapezoid or its fits. Gain with the default 0.98 x 0.98 cross-pol and match terms.

f/D = 0.3, -8 dB edge taper: a cos^0.460 feed. Taper and spillover by quadrature of the feed-angle integrals (scipy quad), beamwidth and first sidelobe by a numerical Hankel transform of the aperture field - not the spec's trapezoid or its fits. Gain with the default 0.98 x 0.98 cross-pol and match terms.

references: Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 8
Ruze, Antenna Tolerance Theory, Proc. IEEE 54(4), 1966
archetypes.notes: ONE FEED PATTERN, NOT FOUR ASSUMPTIONS. Illumination efficiency, spillover, beamwidth and sidelobe level were four separately asserted numbers, but all four follow from one feed pattern and the dish's f/D. They are now derived from the classic Silver model: a rotationally symmetric feed with power pattern 2(n+1)cos^n(theta), n set by the edge taper, and physical-optics aperture theory. The edge taper - total, including the path-length spreading (1 + cos theta)/2 - fixes n; spillover is 1 - cos^(n+1)(theta0) exactly; the taper efficiency is the aperture efficiency cot^2(theta0/2) |int sqrt(G) tan(theta/2) dtheta|^2 over the spillover; beamwidth and first sidelobe come from the Hankel transform of the aperture field. Two routes - that feed-angle integral and a direct integration over the aperture - agree to five figures, and a cos^2 feed reproduces the classic optimum, 0.829 at theta0 = 66 deg and -10.9 dB edge taper. WHAT WAS WRONG. The old defaults, eta_ill = 0.82 and eta_spill = 0.85, counted spillover twice: 0.82 is the classic optimum of the PRODUCT of taper and spillover. At f/D = 0.4 and -11 dB the model splits it 0.886 x 0.933 = 0.827, against the old 0.697 - 0.74 dB of gain the old budget lost. The beamwidth coefficient there is 66.5 lambda/D, not 70, and the first sidelobe -25.2 dB, not an indicative -24. The -11 dB optimum holds for f/D from 0.4 to 0.6 (the best edge taper runs -10.4 to -10.9 dB) and moves to about -9 dB at f/D = 0.3.

archetypes.name: Cassegrain dual reflector
archetypes.summary: Paraboloid with a hyperboloidal subreflector, folding the feed back to the vertex.

parameters.name: illumination efficiency
parameters.description: Taper efficiency. DERIVED from the edge taper and the equivalent paraboloid; supply it to override.

parameters.name: spillover efficiency
parameters.description: Spillover past the subreflector. DERIVED likewise; supply it to override.

parameters.name: magnification
parameters.description: equivalent focal length divided by the main reflector's

parameters.name: edge taper
parameters.description: total illumination at the main rim relative to the centre, spreading included

parameters.name: blockage half-angle
parameters.description: feed angle whose ray lands at the edge of the subreflector's shadow

synthesis.notes: feed power the subreflector intercepts, exact for a 2(n+1)cos^n feed
taper efficiency of the equivalent paraboloid's aperture field
Ds/D in tenths - 1 at the default. Kept away from zero on purpose: a fit variable that is exactly zero at the default is floating-point noise to the scale audit.

analysis.expr: (1 - np.trapezoid(np.cos(np.linspace(0, dual_theta_b, 4001))**(dual_n/2)*np.tan(np.linspace(0, dual_theta_b, 4001)/2), np.linspace(0, dual_theta_b, 4001))/np.trapezoid(np.cos(np.linspace(0, dual_theta_f, 4001))**(dual_n/2)*np.tan(np.linspace(0, dual_theta_f, 4001)/2), np.linspace(0, dual_theta_f, 4001)))**2
analysis.notes: Geometric-optics blockage: the square of the fraction of the aperture FIELD outside the subreflector's shadow. The old (1 - (Ds/D)^2)^2 assumed uniform illumination and understated the loss - 0.965 against 0.980 at Ds/D = 0.1. Feed and strut blockage are not included.
From the Hankel transform of the blocked equivalent aperture, fitted over edge taper -20..-3 dB, equivalent f/D 0.8..3.0 and Ds/D 0..0.2. Held-out error under 0.05 lambda/D.

From the Hankel transform of the blocked equivalent aperture, fitted over edge taper -20..-3 dB, equivalent f/D 0.8..3.0 and Ds/D 0..0.2. The PEAK sidelobe: blockage raises the sidelobes and can move the peak off the first lobe. Held-out error under 0.3 dB.
Ds/D below about 0.1 makes subreflector diffraction severe; above 0.15 blockage dominates. Most designs sit between.
HYPERBOLA, so e > 1, from M = (e+1)/(e-1). The Gregorian's ellipse inverts this.

validity: Ds must be at least several wavelengths or diffraction invalidates ray optics
the feed sees the subreflector, so feed taper is set by the subreflector subtended angle, not the main reflector's
advantage over prime focus is short feed runs and low spillover onto warm ground (lower noise temperature), not raw gain
magnification is a design input here, not derived from the subreflector position; it previously sat in this spec as a hard-coded 1.0, which was a placeholder rather than a result

eta_ill, eta_spill, eta_blockage, hpbw_deg and peak_sidelobe_db are geometric-optics results for a rotationally symmetric cos^n feed: subreflector diffraction, which matters once Ds is only a few wavelengths, and feed and strut blockage are not in them

known_cases.source: Ds/D = 0.1 gives (1-0.01)^2 = 0.9801 blockage efficiency. Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 8 Blockage now from rays traced through the real subreflector at the default -11 dB edge taper: the shadowed disc holds the brightest field, so 0.9652 rather than the uniform-illumination 0.9801.
M = 4 gives e = (4+1)/(4-1) = 1.667 for the hyperboloid and an equivalent f/D of 1.4, so the feed illuminates only 20.25 deg. Hannan, IRE T-AP 9(2), 1961

M 4.0, f/D 0.35, Ds/D 0.1, -11 dB edge taper: efficiencies from rays TRACED through the real hyperboloid and main dish with power conserved along ray tubes (otahub.num.paraboloid); beamwidth and peak sidelobe by Hankel transform of the blocked aperture - not the spec's feed-angle integrals or its fits.

M 2.5, f/D 0.4, Ds/D 0.15, -9 dB edge taper: efficiencies from rays TRACED through the real hyperboloid and main dish with power conserved along ray tubes (otahub.num.paraboloid); beamwidth and peak sidelobe by Hankel transform of the blocked aperture - not the spec's feed-angle integrals or its fits.

M 6.0, f/D 0.3, Ds/D 0.05, -14 dB edge taper: efficiencies from rays TRACED through the real hyperboloid and main dish with power conserved along ray tubes (otahub.num.paraboloid); beamwidth and peak sidelobe by Hankel transform of the blocked aperture - not the spec's feed-angle integrals or its fits.

references: Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 8
archetypes.notes: ONE EQUIVALENT PARABOLOID, VERIFIED BY RAY TRACING. In geometric optics a Cassegrain or Gregorian illuminates its main aperture exactly as a single paraboloid of focal length M*F would, fed by the same feed. That was traced ray by ray through the real hyperboloid and ellipsoid, not assumed: tan(psi/2)/tan(theta/2) equals M = (e+1)/(e-1) or (1+e)/(1-e) to nine figures. So the prime-focus derivation carries over at the feed's rim angle theta_f = 2 atan(1/(4 M f/D)): n from the edge taper, spillover past the subreflector exactly 1 - cos^(n+1)(theta_f), taper efficiency from the feed-angle integral. A direct integration over the traced aperture mapping agrees to five figures. BLOCKAGE. The old (1 - (Ds/D)^2)^2 assumes uniform illumination; the subreflector in fact shadows the brightest part of the aperture. The shadowed field fraction, I(theta_b)/I(theta_f) with I the same field integral, gives 0.965 at Ds/D = 0.1 where the uniform rule gave 0.980, and 0.930 at 0.15 against 0.956. WHAT CHANGED. The old 0.85 x 0.90 taper and spillover were asserted; at the default geometry and -11 dB edge taper they are 0.885 and 0.921, so with the corrected blockage the budget rises 0.21 dB. The beamwidth and PEAK sidelobe now include the blockage, which is what raises a Cassegrain's sidelobes above a prime-focus dish's.

archetypes.name: 90-degree corner reflector
archetypes.summary: Dipole on the bisector of two 90-degree plates, solved as a four-element image array including the mutual coupling that sets the feed resistance.

parameters.name: driven element radius / lambda
parameters.description: radius of the half-wave dipole; sets its driving-point impedance, not the directivity

synthesis.notes: plates of about twice the vertex spacing; beyond that the extra gain is marginal

analysis.notes: FIELD factor at boresight. Images: two negative at +-90 deg and one positive at 180 deg, all at radius S, giving 2*cos(kS) - 2. Maximum 4.0 at S = lambda/2; the null is at S = lambda, not lambda/2.

analysis.expr: (eta0/(4*pi))*(2*Ci(k0*sqrt(2)*S) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((sqrt(2)*S)**2 + Ld**2) + Ld)) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((sqrt(2)*S)**2 + Ld**2) - Ld)))
analysis.notes: to each of the two negative images, at spacing sqrt(2)*S
to the positive double-reflection image, at spacing 2*S

Signs follow the image currents. This is the figure that actually limits how close to the vertex the dipole can go: at S = 0.25 lambda it is 27 ohm, at 0.1 lambda under 1 ohm. This is the INDUCED-EMF resistance: an assumed sinusoid on an exactly half-wave element. It is what the directivity formula needs, and there it is right - the directivity below is within 0.04 dB of the exact image solution everywhere tested. It is NOT what the feed sees; input_resistance_ohm is.

Driving-point resistance of the half-wave element in the corner. Solved, not assumed: the dipole and its image set as one method-of-moments problem (otahub.num.corner), exact for infinite plates and using the real current. Fitted over S = 0.1..1.0 lambda and aw = 1e-4..5e-3 lambda (444 solves): grid residual under 1.3 ohm, and within 2.2 ohm of fresh solves at radii and spacings the fit never saw. The solver's own mesh uncertainty on the fattest wire is 2-3 ohm.

Driving-point reactance of the same element - large and inductive over most of the range, because a half-wave element is longer than resonant and the corner's images add reactance of their own. Resonating it means shortening it, to anywhere from 0.42 to 0.52 lambda depending on spacing and radius. Solved, not assumed: the dipole and its image set as one method-of-moments problem (otahub.num.corner), exact for infinite plates and using the real current. Fitted over S = 0.1..1.0 lambda and aw = 1e-4..5e-3 lambda (444 solves): grid residual under 1.3 ohm, and within 2.2 ohm of fresh solves at radii and spacings the fit never saw. The solver's own mesh uncertainty on the fattest wire is 2-3 ohm.

D = |AF|^2 * D_dipole * R_isolated/R_in. The mutual-coupling term is what brings the answer to the measured ~12 dBi; omitting it overstates the gain by 2 dB at S = lambda/2. Checked against the exact image-MoM solution: within 0.04 dB from S = 0.1 to 0.75 lambda (90 deg) and 0.35 to 0.8 (60 deg).

validity: plates assumed INFINITE and perfectly conducting. Real plates of about 2S truncate the images, and that - not the array factor - is what makes very small spacings perform poorly
with infinite plates the directivity is nearly flat from S = 0.05 to 0.5 lambda (12.6 down to 11.8 dBi); the feed resistance, not the pattern, chooses the spacing
S = lambda is a true boresight null, where all four images cancel
half-wave driven element assumed by the mutual-impedance formula

input_resistance_ohm and input_reactance_ohm hold for S = 0.1..1.0 lambda and element radius 1e-4..5e-3 lambda, for the exactly half-wave element this spec designs, with infinite plates. Near the vertex the resistance is a few ohms under 40-100 ohm of reactance: that, not the pattern, is what makes close spacing hard to feed

known_cases.source: S = lambda/2 maximises the boresight array factor at 4.0 (NOT a null). With the mutual terms the feed sees 126 ohm and the directivity is 15.19 (11.81 dBi), the textbook ~12 dBi for a 90-degree corner. Image sum verified to leave 1e-15 of tangential E on the plates.
At S = lambda the four images cancel exactly at boresight. This is the real null; the previous version of this spec placed it at lambda/2, which is where the optimum actually is.
Quarter-wave spacing: |AF| = 2*(1-cos(pi/2)) = 2. The feed resistance has fallen to 27 ohm, which is the practical reason not to go closer.

Direct method-of-moments solve of the dipole and its image set (otahub.num.corner, exact kernel, 40 segments), not the fit: 151.3 + j49.3 ohm at S = 0.5 lambda, radius 0.001 lambda. The fit it checks is good to 2.2 ohm on points it never saw.

Direct method-of-moments solve of the dipole and its image set (otahub.num.corner, exact kernel, 40 segments), not the fit: 35.7 + j107.0 ohm at S = 0.25 lambda, radius 0.001 lambda. The fit it checks is good to 2.2 ohm on points it never saw.

Direct method-of-moments solve of the dipole and its image set (otahub.num.corner, exact kernel, 40 segments), not the fit: 58.8 + j114.6 ohm at S = 0.3 lambda, radius 0.0003 lambda. The fit it checks is good to 2.2 ohm on points it never saw.

references: Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 15.3 (corner reflectors) and eq. 8-72 (mutual impedance)
Image set and array factor verified here numerically against the plate boundary condition

archetypes.name: 60-degree corner reflector
archetypes.summary: Narrower corner, six image sources instead of four, and about 2.5 dB more gain than the 90-degree version.

parameters.name: driven element radius / lambda
parameters.description: radius of the half-wave dipole; sets its driving-point impedance, not the directivity

analysis.notes: Six sources at 60-degree steps with alternating sign sum to 2j*[sin(kS) - 2*sin(kS/2)] on boresight. Peaks near S = 0.7 lambda at 5.14, against the 90-degree corner's best of 4.0.

analysis.expr: self_resistance_ohm - 2*(eta0/(4*pi))*(2*Ci(k0*S) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((S)**2 + Ld**2) + Ld)) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((S)**2 + Ld**2) - Ld))) + 2*(eta0/(4*pi))*(2*Ci(k0*sqrt(3)*S) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((sqrt(3)*S)**2 + Ld**2) + Ld)) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((sqrt(3)*S)**2 + Ld**2) - Ld))) - (eta0/(4*pi))*(2*Ci(k0*2*S) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((2*S)**2 + Ld**2) + Ld)) - Ci(k0*(sqrt((2*S)**2 + Ld**2) - Ld)))
analysis.notes: Images sit at 60-degree steps on a circle of radius S, so the spacings to the driven element are S, sqrt(3)*S and 2*S, with signs -, + and - following the image currents. This is the INDUCED-EMF resistance: an assumed sinusoid on an exactly half-wave element. It is what the directivity formula needs, and there it is right - the directivity below is within 0.04 dB of the exact image solution everywhere tested. It is NOT what the feed sees; input_resistance_ohm is.

Driving-point resistance of the half-wave element in the corner. Solved, not assumed: the dipole and its image set as one method-of-moments problem (otahub.num.corner), exact for infinite plates and using the real current. Fitted over S = 0.1..1.0 lambda and aw = 1e-4..5e-3 lambda (444 solves): grid residual under 1.3 ohm, and within 2.2 ohm of fresh solves at radii and spacings the fit never saw. The solver's own mesh uncertainty on the fattest wire is 2-3 ohm.

Driving-point reactance of the same element - large and inductive over most of the range, because a half-wave element is longer than resonant and the corner's images add reactance of their own. Resonating it means shortening it, to anywhere from 0.42 to 0.52 lambda depending on spacing and radius. Solved, not assumed: the dipole and its image set as one method-of-moments problem (otahub.num.corner), exact for infinite plates and using the real current. Fitted over S = 0.1..1.0 lambda and aw = 1e-4..5e-3 lambda (444 solves): grid residual under 1.3 ohm, and within 2.2 ohm of fresh solves at radii and spacings the fit never saw. The solver's own mesh uncertainty on the fattest wire is 2-3 ohm.
Checked against the exact image-MoM solution: within 0.04 dB from S = 0.1 to 0.75 lambda (90 deg) and 0.35 to 0.8 (60 deg).
against the best 90-degree corner, S = lambda/2 at 11.81 dBi

validity: infinite perfectly conducting plates, as for the 90-degree case
the corner angle must divide 180 exactly for the image construction to close; 60, 45 and 36 degrees do, 70 does not
S = lambda is again a boresight null
narrower corners need physically longer plates for the same truncation error, which is why 90 degrees remains the common choice

input_resistance_ohm and input_reactance_ohm hold for S = 0.1..1.0 lambda and element radius 1e-4..5e-3 lambda, for the exactly half-wave element this spec designs, with infinite plates. Near the vertex the resistance is a few ohms under 40-100 ohm of reactance: that, not the pattern, is what makes close spacing hard to feed

known_cases.source: Numerical sum over the six image sources gives |AF| = 5.1382 at S = 0.7 lambda, and the image set leaves 2e-15 of tangential E on the plates. With mutual coupling the directivity is 21.51 (13.33 dBi).
At half-wave spacing the 60-degree corner already matches the 90-degree corner's best array factor while its feed resistance is only 71 ohm, so the directivity is 2.5 dB higher
sin(2*pi) - 2*sin(pi) = 0: the same S = lambda null as the 90-degree corner

Direct method-of-moments solve of the dipole and its image set (otahub.num.corner, exact kernel, 40 segments), not the fit: 173.9 + j38.9 ohm at S = 0.7 lambda, radius 0.001 lambda. The fit it checks is good to 2.2 ohm on points it never saw.

Direct method-of-moments solve of the dipole and its image set (otahub.num.corner, exact kernel, 40 segments), not the fit: 111.3 + j148.0 ohm at S = 0.5 lambda, radius 0.002 lambda. The fit it checks is good to 2.2 ohm on points it never saw.

references: Image construction verified numerically against the plate boundary condition

archetypes.name: Offset-fed parabolic reflector
archetypes.summary: A slice of a paraboloid taken off the axis, so the feed and its struts sit outside the aperture and block nothing.

parameters.name: aperture diameter
parameters.description: projected circular aperture

parameters.name: parent focal ratio
parameters.description: focal length of the parent paraboloid divided by the aperture diameter

parameters.name: offset height ratio
parameters.description: height of the aperture centre above the parent axis, over D. Must exceed 0.5 for clearance.

parameters.name: illumination efficiency
parameters.description: Taper efficiency. DERIVED from the feed taper and geometry; supply it to override.

parameters.name: spillover efficiency
parameters.description: Spillover efficiency. DERIVED from the feed taper and geometry; supply it to override.

parameters.name: feed taper at the rim
parameters.description: the feed pattern's own level at the rim cone, relative to its axis. Unlike the prime-focus dish's edge taper this excludes spreading loss, which differs between the upper and lower rim

synthesis.notes: exact: the rim is a circular cone of half-angle theta* about the feed axis

Taper efficiency from a 2-D integration of cos^(n/2)(psi)/r over the projected aperture, fitted over feed taper -20..-3 dB, parent f/D 0.3..1.0 and h0/D 0.55..1.2 (864 points): within 0.003 on the grid and 0.0013 on points it never saw.

analysis.notes: gap between the lower rim and the parent axis. Zero or negative means the feed is back in the beam and the offset has bought nothing.
Angle from the focal axis to the upper rim. On a paraboloid a point at radius r subtends 2*atan(r/2F) from the focus - exact, not an approximation.
tilt of the feed axis from the parent axis - the bisector of the two rim angles
half-angle the aperture subtends at the feed; this is what sets the required feed taper
Exactly one, by construction. This is the entire reason for the offset geometry, and it also removes the blockage-scattered sidelobes.

Mean of the two principal planes, from the 2-D Fourier transform of the aperture field and fitted to 0.09 lambda/D (0.03 on held-out points); the planes differ by under 2%. 67.4 lambda/D at the default design, not the asserted 70.
Taper efficiency against a SYMMETRIC dish with the same feed and rim angle - the cost of the tilted illumination. Negative.

Against a prime-focus dish with the same feed and rim angle and a 0.1 D blockage: the 0.09 dB of blockage recovered, less the taper penalty. Negative at short and moderate focal lengths - -0.11 dB at the default design, down to -0.75 dB at parent f/D = 0.3 - about even at 0.7-0.8, and at most +0.07 dB for long, gently offset dishes. The offset buys sidelobes and noise temperature, not gain.

validity: h0 > D/2, or there is no clearance and the geometry is not actually offset

a linearly polarised feed on an offset reflector generates two cross-polar lobes in the plane of asymmetry; this spec does not quantify them. A circularly polarised feed avoids the cross-pol but squints the beam instead
ray optics: D must be many wavelengths

eta_ill, eta_spill and hpbw_deg follow a rotationally symmetric cos^n feed aimed along the rim-cone axis, scalar aperture theory; they hold for feed taper -20..-3 dB, parent f/D 0.3..1.0 and h0/D 0.55..1.2. Depolarisation of a linear feed is not in them - supply measured efficiencies to override

known_cases.source: Exact paraboloid geometry: a rim point at radius r subtends 2*atan(r/2F). With F = 0.5 m, the rims at 1.1 m and 0.1 m give 95.452 and 11.421 deg, so the feed tilts 53.44 deg and sees a 42.02 deg half-angle.
Blockage efficiency is exactly 1 by construction: the feed sits below the lower rim, out of the reflected beam.

Parent f/D 0.5, h0/D 0.6, -10 dB feed taper (cos^7.750): taper efficiency and both beamwidths by 2-D integration over the projected aperture (otahub.num.paraboloid), spillover and the symmetric comparison by quadrature of the feed-angle integrals - not the spec's fits.

The same design against a symmetric dish with the same feed and rim angle - taper efficiency by 2-D aperture integration against the feed-angle quadrature - held to 0.01 dB absolute, because a near-zero dB difference makes a relative tolerance meaningless.

Parent f/D 0.4, h0/D 0.8, -12 dB feed taper (cos^11.707): taper efficiency and both beamwidths by 2-D integration over the projected aperture (otahub.num.paraboloid), spillover and the symmetric comparison by quadrature of the feed-angle integrals - not the spec's fits.

The same design against a symmetric dish with the same feed and rim angle - taper efficiency by 2-D aperture integration against the feed-angle quadrature - held to 0.01 dB absolute, because a near-zero dB difference makes a relative tolerance meaningless.

Parent f/D 0.7, h0/D 1.0, -8 dB feed taper (cos^15.574): taper efficiency and both beamwidths by 2-D integration over the projected aperture (otahub.num.paraboloid), spillover and the symmetric comparison by quadrature of the feed-angle integrals - not the spec's fits.

The same design against a symmetric dish with the same feed and rim angle - taper efficiency by 2-D aperture integration against the feed-angle quadrature - held to 0.01 dB absolute, because a near-zero dB difference makes a relative tolerance meaningless.

references: Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 8.5 (offset reflectors)
Rusch & Potter, Analysis of Reflector Antennas, Academic Press 1970
Chu & Turrin, Depolarization properties of offset reflector antennas, IEEE T-AP 21(3), 1973
archetypes.notes: FROM THE FEED, AS FOR THE PRIME-FOCUS DISH. Seen from the focus, the rim of an offset paraboloid is a circular cone about the bisector of the upper and lower rim angles - checked numerically, not assumed: every rim ray sits at theta* from that axis to 1e-14 rad. So a feed aimed along it, with power pattern 2(n+1)cos^n and n set by the feed taper at the rim, has spillover exactly 1 - cos^(n+1)(theta*). The taper efficiency does NOT carry over from the symmetric dish: the lower rim is much closer to the feed than the upper, so the spherical spreading tilts the aperture illumination. The symmetric formula with theta* overstates it by 1% at long focal lengths and up to 20% at f/D = 0.3. It is fitted instead to a 2-D integration over the projected aperture (otahub.num.paraboloid), as is the beamwidth, whose two principal planes differ by under 2%. WHAT CHANGED. The old defaults were the prime-focus ones, 0.82 x 0.85 = 0.697, with spillover counted twice. At the default geometry the best feed taper is -9.6 dB for a product of 0.780; the new default, -10 dB, gives 0.779, and 0.48 dB more gain than the old budget. And the offset's 'gain advantage over prime focus' - the 0.09 dB of a 10% blockage recovered - was never the whole story. Against a symmetric dish with the same feed and rim angle, the tilted illumination costs taper efficiency, and over the fitted range the offset comes out up to 0.75 dB BEHIND at parent f/D = 0.3, 0.09-0.22 dB behind at the default 0.5, about even at 0.7-0.8, and ahead by at most 0.07 dB at f/D = 1. Its prize is the sidelobes and noise temperature, as the old note said; now the numbers say it too.

archetypes.notes: ONE EQUIVALENT PARABOLOID, VERIFIED BY RAY TRACING. In geometric optics a Cassegrain or Gregorian illuminates its main aperture exactly as a single paraboloid of focal length M*F would, fed by the same feed. That was traced ray by ray through the real hyperboloid and ellipsoid, not assumed: tan(psi/2)/tan(theta/2) equals M = (e+1)/(e-1) or (1+e)/(1-e) to nine figures. So the prime-focus derivation carries over at the feed's rim angle theta_f = 2 atan(1/(4 M f/D)): n from the edge taper, spillover past the subreflector exactly 1 - cos^(n+1)(theta_f), taper efficiency from the feed-angle integral. A direct integration over the traced aperture mapping agrees to five figures. BLOCKAGE. The old (1 - (Ds/D)^2)^2 assumes uniform illumination; the subreflector in fact shadows the brightest part of the aperture. The shadowed field fraction, I(theta_b)/I(theta_f) with I the same field integral, gives 0.965 at Ds/D = 0.1 where the uniform rule gave 0.980, and 0.930 at 0.15 against 0.956. WHAT CHANGED. The old 0.85 x 0.90 taper and spillover were asserted; at the default geometry and -11 dB edge taper they are 0.885 and 0.921, so with the corrected blockage the budget rises 0.21 dB. The beamwidth and PEAK sidelobe now include the blockage, which is what raises a Cassegrain's sidelobes above a prime-focus dish's.

archetypes.notes: FROM THE LINE FEED, ONE DIMENSION DOWN FROM THE DISH. Across the focusing plane the line feed launches a cylindrical wave with transverse power pattern cos^n(theta); it spreads as 1/sqrt(r), not 1/r, so the aperture field is sqrt(cos^n(theta)/r) with r = 2F/(1 + cos theta). The taper efficiency is then [int cos^(n/2)/sqrt(1 + cos) dtheta]^2 / (tan(theta0/2) int cos^n dtheta), evaluated in the spec; the spillover is the fraction of the feed's transverse power the reflector intercepts. A direct integration over the aperture coordinate agrees to six figures, and the uniform limit reproduces the uniform line source's 50.8 lambda/W and -13.3 dB. WHAT CHANGED. The old budget, 0.81 x 0.88 = 0.713, understated a line-fed cylinder by about 1 dB: at f/W = 0.4 the product peaks at 0.900. And the dish's -11 dB rule does not carry over - a line aperture wants a LIGHTER taper, -6.5 to -8.5 dB for f/W 0.3-0.7, so the default is -8 dB. The focusing-plane beamwidth there is 57.9 lambda/W, not the dish's 70, which makes the default fan beam 3.4:1 rather than 4.1:1.
